messages.author: e1aed7f6ccf84b4b
messages.subject: pcount() and interpreting coefficients
parts:
Hi all,
I'm using the pcount() function in unmarked to investigate relationships between birds and vegetation features/cover types at the point count locations. The coefficients of my best models include tree height and cover type. Tree height has a positive association with abundance (beta coefficient: 0.189). The cover types from highest abundance to lowest are: Rubber, Teak, Hardwood, Forest. That all seems good to me. 

The confusing part is that mean tree heights are different in the four cover types. Mean tree heights from highest to lowest are: Forest, Hardwood, Rubber, Teak. Forest/Hardwood and Rubber/Teak aren't statistically different, but all other pairs are using one-way ANOVAs and Tukey's HSD tests.

Put together, these results say that taller trees are associated with abundance, but that cover types with shorter trees have the highest abundance. I think this means that within a cover type, the points near taller trees are associated with higher avian abundance. It seems a bit counter-intuitive though, so I'm not quite certain I'm interpreting it correctly. Has anyone else found these sort of seemingly contradictory results and any suggestions on how to explain it?

Thanks!
-Wendy

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] pcount() and interpreting coefficients
parts:
Dear Wendy,

I think that your interpretation is correct. I assume that you have added both the habitat type factor and the vegetation covariate alongside in your model ? What are their coefficients when they're both in the model ?

Note that your problem is a general one about the interpretation of the coefficients of a covariate and a factor that are correlated, i.e., this is a general regression problem not specific to the Poisson regression which is part of the Nmix model. I think that you don't necessarily have a contradiction: wouldn't it be possible that the abundance pattern in vegetation types could be related to something other than mere height ?

Have you checked for the interaction between type and height ? Perhaps the effect of height is not the same in every type.

Best regards  -- Marc

Hi Marc, 
Yep, both habitat and tree height are in the model. I did a backwards selection process using AICc to determine our candidate set of variables, then ran all possible combinations of the variables to find our best model(s). We are somewhat limited in data - 30 points per cover type - so are planning to analyze with interaction terms after next year's field season when more points will be visited and hopefully that will help make the relationships clearer! I did a quick check with the data we have and the interaction does improve AICc, although not by > 2 units, and the relationships make sense given my knowledge of the system.

Is there a way to check or account for correlations between continuous and factor covariates?

Thanks for your response!
-Wendy

messages.author: d3fd439c2e48caf1
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] pcount() and interpreting coefficients
parts:
I'd say the simplest way to check for an association between a factor and a continuous covariate with a boxplot, e.g. boxplot(continuousVariable~categoricalVariable, data).

I come up against this issue often and typically test these association with a kruskal-wallis test, e.g. kruskal.test(continuousVariable~categoricalVariable, data). I don't know of a "rule of thumb" for determining how much redundancy between a categorical and continuous covariate is too much (e.g. something akin to the r < 0.6/0.7 for two continuous covariates), but if the kruskal test is highly significant, the two covariates likely explain much of the same variation.

If you want to "remove" the correlated information, oftentimes people will make a new continuous covariate based on the residuals of the relationship, e.g. data$residContinuous = resid(lm(continuousVariable~categoricalVariable, data)), however results are less easily interpreted.

Hope that helps

Giancarlo
